Syncopation. The displacement of normal metrical accent, placing emphasis on weak beats or off-beats, creating rhythmic tension and surprise. It disrupts the expected regular pulse, pulling against the underlying meter, and is central to jazz, ragtime, blues, and many modern musical idioms.

The simplest syncopation is an accent on beat two or beat four of a four-four measure instead of the expected beats one and three. Offbeat syncopation plays a note on the and of the count—the halfway point between beats—creating a lilting, swinging feel. The Charleston and swing music rely heavily on this effect. Anticipation is another form of syncopation, where a note is played before its expected beat, usually tied across the beat, creating forward motion.

Ragtime composers like Scott Joplin used syncopation to give their marches a dance-like, propulsive quality. Jazz inherited and elaborated the technique as a core feature of its style. But syncopation requires a listener to perceive a background meter—the expected pulse—against which the syncopated rhythm stands out. Without that awareness, syncopation is lost. The rhythmic freedom and syncopation are what mark jazz as its own musical tradition, distinct from the broader study of how musical time is organized through rhythm and beat, with which syncopation disrupts regular rhythmic expectation.
